theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Explain the parable of the sower and the interpretation which Jesus gave of it in Mark 4:1-20.
theory.idealAnswer:
The parable of the sower stands at the head of Mark's collection of parables depicting the character of God's kingdom, and the syllabus reads it as an explanation of the opposition Jesus met. The reason why Jesus was opposed by the religious leaders and others, including His own relations, was the spiritual condition of their hearts, and in the parable He urged His hearers to give careful consideration to the nature of their own hearts. Some hearers never understood or grasped His message at all; others were discouraged through difficulties; others again were seduced through prosperity; the result was that only a limited proportion became lastingly committed to it.

Before explaining the parable Jesus answered the disciples' question as to why He employed parables. The essence of His reply is that He did so in order to test the spiritual responsiveness of His audience. Those provoked by the parables into intensive reflection could proceed to obtain enlightenment concerning them, while those who would not reflect on them could be ever seeing but never perceiving; that is, they would understand the literal meaning of the words but not the parable's deeper significance.

In the interpretation the farmer, or sower, probably represents Jesus and all who sow or proclaim the word of God, which is the seed. The kinds of soil represent four different ways in which people respond to God's word, three of them negative. The first is hard-hearted indifference, where Satan, like the birds, comes immediately and takes the word away, so that in effect there is no response. The second is a hasty, enthusiastic but shallow profession of acceptance which lasts only a short time because the word takes no root; there is a lack of spiritual depth, and when trouble or persecution comes on account of the word such hearers quickly fall away, their profession proving not to be genuine. The third are those who hear the word but are preoccupied with the cares and riches of this life, which choke the word and make it unfruitful, indicating that they are not true believers. By contrast others hear the word, accept it - welcome it for themselves - and produce a crop. These are evidently genuine disciples who bear fruitful yields of varying amounts: thirty, sixty or a hundredfold.

Hearers are urged to consider the nature of their own hearts
Jesus taught in parables to test the spiritual responsiveness of His audience
Those who would not reflect would be ever seeing but never perceiving
The sower represents Jesus and all who proclaim the word; the seed is the word of God
Hard-hearted indifference: Satan, like the birds, takes the word away at once
Shallow, rootless profession falls away when trouble or persecution comes

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Give an account of Jesus' teaching on marriage and divorce in Mark 10:1-12, and explain why He referred the Pharisees back to the creation.
theory.idealAnswer:
The syllabus stresses that the question put by the Pharisees was malicious. It was put to Jesus in order to test Him, that is, to try to induce Him to incriminate Himself by contradicting the Mosaic Law. The Mosaic enactment of Deuteronomy 24:1-4 stated that a husband was allowed to divorce his wife by writing and giving to her a certificate of divorce if he had found some unseemly thing in her, and the whole question turned upon what constituted an unseemly thing.

Shammai and Hillel were the authorities in the interpretation of the Mosaic Law, and different groups took their authority from them. The school of Shammai maintained the strict interpretation, holding that the marriage band was indissoluble except in the event of the wife's infidelity. The school of Hillel took the liberal view, allowing divorce for almost any cause. To answer either school directly would have set Jesus against a recognised body of opinion, which is what His questioners intended.

In reply Jesus first pointed out that Moses' legislation was a concession to human weakness, rightly introduced to regulate divorce in a defective state of society. He quoted the words, 'Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote to you this commandment.' Moses' provision was therefore not a divine ideal but a restraint upon an existing evil.

Secondly, Jesus took the Pharisees back beyond Moses to God's ideal at the beginning of creation. From that ideal we discover that marriage was instituted as the divine ideal for man and woman, and that the bond is permanent and indissoluble. By going behind the concession to the creation ordinance Jesus set the discussion on a different footing altogether: the question is not how much divorce the Law will tolerate, but what God intended marriage to be from the beginning. The passage that follows, on receiving the kingdom in childlike trust, continues the same emphasis upon the divine order rather than upon human casuistry.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Give an account of the trial of Jesus before the Sanhedrin as presented in Mark 14:53-65.
theory.idealAnswer:
The syllabus explains that this trial by the Sanhedrin, the Jewish Supreme Court, had two phases: a small group met at night and the full Council met at daybreak. Jesus was tried for religious offences such as calling Himself the Son of God, which according to the Law was blasphemy. The trial was obviously fixed, because these religious leaders had already decided to kill Jesus.

The Sanhedrin began their deliberations by seeking evidence against Jesus in order to justify a death sentence, but they found none. Many witnesses testified falsely, but their testimonies did not corroborate. In Jewish trials the witnesses served as the prosecution and gave their testimonies separately, and to convict a person the Mosaic Law required precise agreement in the testimony of at least two witnesses.

The claim on which the false witnesses finally agreed twisted Jesus' actual words. He did not say, 'I will destroy this Temple'; He said, 'Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up', and He was speaking not about Herod's Temple but about His own death and resurrection. To this first accusation Jesus gave no response, because the evidence itself was confusing and erroneous, and not answering was wiser than trying to clarify fabricated accusations.

The high priest then asked, 'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?' To refuse to answer this would have been taken as a denial of His mission. Jesus' answer predicted a powerful role-reversal: sitting at the right hand of God meant that He would come to judge them and that they would be answering questions. By tearing his clothes the high priest showed that he regarded this bold declaration as blasphemy; this symbolic expression of horror and indignation was required of the high priest whenever he heard blasphemy, and his reaction also expressed relief, since Jesus' self-incriminating answer removed the need for more witnesses. Without further investigation the high priest called for a verdict, and since there were no objections they all condemned Him as worthy of death. Thereafter some members showed their contempt through mockery and physical abuse, spat in His face - an act of gross personal insult - blindfolded Him on account of His messianic claims, struck Him with their fists and demanded that He prophesy who hit Him.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Describe the supernatural events which accompanied the death of Jesus in Mark 15 and explain the significance the syllabus attaches to them.
theory.idealAnswer:
Mark records five supernatural events that accompanied the death of Jesus: the darkness, Jesus' cry 'My God, my God', His loud cry, the tearing of the temple curtain from top to bottom, and the confession of the Roman centurion.

Jesus hung on the cross for three hours in the daylight, from nine in the morning until noon, and then at the sixth hour total darkness engulfed the whole land, that is Palestine and its environs, until the ninth hour, three in the afternoon. The darkness was probably a cosmic sign of God's judgment on human sin, which was placed on Jesus. It visualised what His cry expressed.

That cry, 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani', is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew of Psalm 22:1, and means 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' The syllabus insists that this was more than a righteous sufferer affirming his faith that the Father would cause him to triumph. Jesus' cry combined abandonment by the Father in a judicial and not a relational sense, together with a genuine affirmation of His relationship to the Father. He was bearing the curse of sin and the Father's judgment upon sin, and experienced for the first time the horror of separation from God, who cannot look on sin and therefore hid His face. Although seemingly exhausted, Jesus was offered vinegar by the soldiers and then uttered a loud cry, after which He breathed His last.

The tearing of the temple curtain carries its own significance. A heavy veil hung in front of the Holy of Holies, a place reserved by God for Himself, and it symbolically separated the Holy God from sinful mankind. The place was entered only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, by the High Priest as he made a sacrifice to gain forgiveness for the sins of all the people. When Jesus died the veil was split in two, showing that His death for our sins had opened the way for us to approach our Holy God. The centurion's confession completes the list, so that a Gentile soldier bears witness to what the religious leaders had denied.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Give an account of the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15:1-35 and state its major conclusions.
theory.idealAnswer:
The syllabus describes the Jerusalem Council as probably the second most significant event in the missionary advance of the Gospel to the Gentiles, the first being the experience Peter went through concerning the conversion of the household of Cornelius and the acceptance of his report by the church in Jerusalem. This second event was crucial because it was to settle for the Gentiles the very critical question of whether one has to become a Jew before he could become a Christian, or whether God accepts us in Christ irrespective of our background. The syllabus draws out the implication for culture and faith: since the Gospel came to us from Europe, must we adopt the European cultural clothing that came with it, or can we be truly African and still be accepted by God in Christ?

The proponents are then set out. Those who belonged to the party of the Pharisees presented their case that the Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses. Peter spoke about the experience he went through in Cornelius' house and how the Gentiles experienced the same outpouring of the Holy Spirit as had occurred to the Jews at Pentecost. Barnabas and Paul spoke about the miraculous signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them. James, the brother of Jesus, who had become an important person among the elders in the church at Jerusalem, gave the speech which clarified the position of the church, and his proposals were accepted.

The conclusions were introduced by the words 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us', which means that they were based on human reasoning and conviction by the Holy Spirit, both agents being important in knowing the will of God when taking decisions. The major conclusions were that the Gentiles were not to be circumcised like the Jews before they could become Christians; that so far as the Law of Moses was concerned they were to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from the eating of blood and from animals whose blood had not been poured out; and that they were to abstain from sexual immorality, since there were even shrine-prostitutes in some Gentile cities. The basis for the food prohibitions was that Gentile Christians must be alert to the sensitivities of their Jewish brethren with whom they might be worshipping. Judas and Silas were sent with Barnabas and Paul to authenticate the letter, and at Antioch the people were glad for its encouraging message.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Describe Paul's ministry in Athens and the two schools of philosophy which he had to address at the Areopagus.
theory.idealAnswer:
Athens was the capital city of the district of Attica in ancient times and the capital of modern Greece, and was named after the patron goddess Athena. In New Testament times Athens could still boast of being one of the most famous centres of wisdom, architecture and art. Though it had been surpassed economically by Corinth and intellectually by Alexandria, the city nevertheless maintained a great reputation.

Three features of the city are singled out. The rocky hill of the Acropolis, about 156 metres high, carried many temples which were centres of worship. West-north-west of the Acropolis lay the Areopagus, which was the seat of Athens' highest court of justice. There was also the Agora, or market place, a large open space surrounded by colonnades, temples, bazaars and government buildings, where the Athenians spent their time discussing political issues and exchanging goods and services.

Besides temple worship, two schools of philosophy reigned in Athens which Paul had to address. The Epicureans, founded by Epicurus (341-270 BC), held a materialistic view of life: death is the end of everything and therefore nothing is to be feared, so the pursuit of happiness was to be the goal of human existence. Paul's message of divine judgment and resurrection was therefore contrary to their beliefs. Stoicism was founded by Zeno of Citium, who taught in a building called the Stoa Poikile in the Agora, from which the school takes its name. In Stoicism the primary focus is on how life is to be lived, with the attainment of virtue stressed above all, virtuous living being living in accordance with nature. Some scholars have contended that the apostle himself was influenced by Stoicism, reflected in letters which stress self-sufficiency, contentment in all circumstances and indifference to whether one is poor or wealthy.

Paul used two approaches. In the synagogue, where there were Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, he used his normal method of proving from the Old Testament Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah. In the market place his approach was different: his message was geared towards moving the audience from what they knew to what they did not know, and was made relevant to their needs. The idol worshippers needed to move from the Unknown God to the Known God, and the philosophers needed to know that there is a God who will judge all the affairs of men after death, which God has proved by raising Jesus from the dead. This pattern of preaching is key to good preaching. Not many converts were won at Athens, as Paul appeared to be in transition, and no church seems to have been established there.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Discuss the chief ideas of Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin and give an account of his death.
theory.idealAnswer:
Stephen's address before the Sanhedrin is sometimes considered as his defence, that is, an answer to the legal charges brought against him, but it is clearly more of an apology: a statement of teaching, or a recital of Old Testament history, climaxing in a stinging rebuke for their murder of Jesus.

Three chief ideas are designed to be emphasised by Stephen's Old Testament story. The first is that the Jewish people throughout their long history have rebelled against God and His accredited messengers. The second is that God does not live in, nor does He desire, a material and fixed shrine or temple: His presence is not confined to sacred sites but accompanies His people, who are to be always a pilgrim church on earth. A subsidiary theme is that the Jewish people have not only rebelled against God and their leaders but have consistently rejected the messengers, or saviours, whom God sent to them, the outstanding proof being their recent rejection of their Messiah.

Other commentators, especially Bruce, suggest two themes running through the speech. The first is that throughout their history God raised up men to act as deliverers of His people, but the Jews repeatedly rejected them and disobeyed the law given by God: after dealing with the establishment of the nation through God's call of Abraham, the speech treats of Joseph, who was rejected by his brothers but rescued by God, and then at greater length of Moses, who came to deliver the people but was rejected by them. The second is that the Jews had the tabernacle in the wilderness and later the temple built by Solomon, but they fell into idolatry and made the mistake of thinking that God actually dwelt in the temple. These two themes are intermingled in the speech.

Stephen's indictment of unbelieving Jews touched his hearers on a tender spot. They became furious, gnashed their teeth at him, and stoned him to death. His death looked more like a lynching than a judicial execution for blasphemy: there was no trial, and Jewish Law had an elaborate arrangement to safeguard the accused person, for if he should recant, or if a witness for the defence should suddenly appear, the stoning must be stopped. It is clear that no such precautions were made for Stephen's benefit. The most impressionable person in this violent scene seems to have been Saul, who looked after the witnesses' clothes and so agreed that Stephen should be stoned; Paul never forgot this awful sight.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Outline the factors which worked to bring to pass Paul's decision of reaching Rome with the Gospel, and describe his dealings with the Jews in Rome.
theory.idealAnswer:
The syllabus lists four factors which brought to pass Paul's decision of reaching Rome with the Gospel. Most important of all was the overruling hand of God, which was obvious throughout the narrative. Secondly, there was the Roman system of governance, which ensured the security and rights of individuals. Thirdly, there was Paul's knowledge and use of his civil rights, seen in his appeal to Caesar and in his appeal to his Roman citizenship when he was about to be flogged. Fourthly, there was Paul's knowledge of the Jewish religion and of the fulfilment of the Jewish hope in the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

Luke traces the journey carefully: from Malta to Syracuse in Sicily, to Rhegium in Italy, to Puteoli, and finally to Rome itself. At Puteoli there were already many Christians, which is significant because it shows that the gospel had already spread from Rome to the Italian seaport. Certainly a church had been planted in Rome by Roman Jews who had gone to the Pentecost feast. Paul accepted the invitation of a Christian fellowship there to spend a week with them. By this time he had evidently become a trusted prisoner and was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him, residing in a rented house.

In Rome, following his principle of speaking first with the Jews, Paul called the Jewish leaders to meet with him because he could not go to their synagogues. He made several points: that he was innocent of damaging the Jews or their customs; that the Roman authorities in Judea thought him innocent; that his only option had been to appeal to Caesar because the Jews refused to deal with him justly; that he was not pressing charges against Israel but only wanted to be acquitted; and that his primary objective in calling them was to talk about the hope of Israel. That hope was more than the resurrection: it meant the fulfilment of the Old Testament promises to Israel, for Paul firmly believed that Jesus is the Messiah of Israel who will return and establish Himself as king of Israel and Lord of the nations.

As on many previous occasions his address divided the people into two camps. As the unconvinced Jews left in disarray Paul applied the words of Isaiah with prophetic insight: obstinate refusal to believe results in calloused hearts, deafened ears and spiritually blinded eyes. Yet while Paul was in Rome during this incarceration the gospel was never hindered. Men may bind preachers, but the gospel cannot be chained; so the kingdom message went from Jew to Gentile and from Jerusalem to Rome.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Explain the problems which had arisen in the churches of Galatia and Paul's purpose in writing the epistle.
theory.idealAnswer:
There was one basic problem disturbing the churches in Galatia: the teaching of the Judaizers. That problem threatened the peace and spiritual welfare of the Christians on two fronts. Firstly, Paul's gospel of justification by faith was threatened by the teaching that Christians, both Gentile and Jew, must keep Moses' law. Secondly, Paul's personal authority as an apostle was attacked, a tactic used to undermine the authenticity of his teachings.

Paul represented the chief obstacle to the success of the Judaizers. As the leader of the mission to the Gentiles his voice carried great weight, and he was as relentless in opposing them as they were in pushing their teaching, saying that to them he did not yield submission even for a moment, that the truth of the gospel might be preserved. In order to prevail they therefore had to destroy his influence, and they attacked him at his Achilles heel: because he was not one of the Twelve apostles, they argued, his authority was not apostolic, and whatever he knew he got second-hand and got it garbled at that.

Paul saw clearly that the issues raised by the subversive activities of the Judaizers had wider implications than the dominant Jewish Christian element realised, and the rapidity with which the Galatians had departed from the freedom of the gospel served as a goad to him, so that he wrote, 'I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting Him who called you by the grace of Christ for a different gospel.'

His purposes may therefore be set out in three parts. He wrote to defend his place and authority as a genuine apostle of Jesus Christ, chiefly in chapters 1 and 2, establishing that his commission and gospel came directly from Jesus and that the gospel he preached had been vindicated before the other apostles. He wrote to correct the error of the Judaizers and to prove the truth of the gospel he preached, in chapters 3 and 4, which includes a demonstration that justification is by faith and not by the law. And he wrote to teach about the Spirit-controlled life that accompanies justification by faith, in chapters 5 and 6, because his detractors seemed to say that his doctrine of grace led to licentiousness; in this last section he appeals to total inward moral change, which may be seen as Paul's ethics. The key word of the epistle is faith and its theme is justification by faith.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Discuss the contrast between law and grace as Paul sets it out in Galatians 5.
theory.idealAnswer:
The last verse of chapter 4 describes the believer's position: he is free. The first verse of chapter 5 refers to his practice: he should live as a free man. Christ leads into glorious freedom, and there is need to preserve it. It is in this setting that Paul illustrates the difference between the law and grace. The law would say, 'if you earn your freedom you will become free'; but grace says, 'you have been made free at the tremendous cost of the death of Christ, now in gratitude to God, you should stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made you free.'

The essential distinction is stated thus: the Law commands but does not enable, whereas grace provides what the law demands and then enables a man to live a life consistent with his position by the power of the Holy Spirit. C. H. Mackintosh has put the same point memorably: 'The Law demands strength from one who has none and curses him if he cannot display it. The Gospel gives strength to one who has none and blesses him in the exhibition of it.'

Paul also teaches in this chapter that legalism - undue respect for the law and legal forms - makes Christ of no value. The Judaizers insisted on the necessity of Gentile believers being circumcised for salvation; Paul insists that to depend on circumcision is to make Christ of no benefit, for if observing a mere ritual could help, then Christ is unnecessary. Legalism moreover requires men to keep the whole Law: one cannot accept the easy commandments and reject the others.

The positive side follows in the teaching on walking by the Spirit. Paul teaches how we may fulfil the just requirements of the law, not by our own strength but by the saving grace which comes through faith in the atoning work of Christ. By believing in Jesus, He fills us with His Holy Spirit, and we live the Christian life controlled by God's Holy Spirit and no longer by our human desires. The Christian who walks by the Spirit therefore does not manifest the desires of the flesh but bears the fruit of the Spirit, and so fulfils the just requirement of the law summed up in the commandment to love one's neighbour as oneself. All the virtues listed constitute one fruit, singular, so that all of them must be manifested in the Christian who lives in the power of the Holy Spirit.

theory.subject: NT
theory.topic: Qualifications Necessary for Spiritual Oversight or the Ministry
theory.question: State the qualifications necessary for spiritual oversight in the church, distinguishing the office of bishop from that of deacon.
theory.idealAnswer:
The seriousness with which Paul regarded the ministry is revealed in the detailed qualifications required of those who were to be appointed to the office of bishop or deacon. His aim was to encourage respect for the congregation's leaders. In general terms, bishops must be men of integrity, sobriety and conscientiousness; and both bishop and deacon should be the husband of one wife and a model of a family head.

The office of bishop is a noble one, and the qualifications required are high and of permanent significance. The bishop must be a man of able mind and excellent character, socially adaptable and tactful, and able to teach and lead. In everything he must be above reproach, including in his marital and family relationships; he must be deeply grounded in the faith and must command the respect of all.

The word 'deacon' means servant or helper, and refers to the bishops' assistant. Deacons take care of the mundane matters of church life - mundane meaning worldly as contrasted with spiritual or heavenly - and particularly the distribution of charity. Like the bishops, deacons must also be men of quality, even though their function in the congregation is significantly different. Deacons should be proved blameless through examination before entering office. The desirable characteristics named are sincerity in speech and faith, sobriety and unselfishness, and their private life ought to manifest a true Christian home. Good service in the diaconate results in higher position and confidence, with consequent influence.

The reference to 'women' in verse 11 may imply a female order of deaconesses, or may refer to deacons' wives, who were expected to help in the charitable work of their husbands. The section closes with the statement of the purpose of the letter, how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household, and with the quotation of an early Christian hymn or creed which traces the career of Christ from incarnation to ascension.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Outline the counter-measures which Paul prescribed to Timothy in 1 Timothy 4:6-16 against the threats to the safety of the church.
theory.idealAnswer:
It is necessary that a good minister instructs the people in sound doctrine, which is the diet of his own soul, and superstition is to be avoided; taboos should have no place in an intelligent Christian approach, in contrast to the many systems of taboos in heathen cults.

The first counter-measure is that the minister should live on his own message. A good minister is not a theorizer: he teaches the apostolic doctrine which he has made his own, both as nourishment by which to live and as a standard by which to judge himself. Secondly, superstition is to be avoided; the church at this stage was confronted with invented stories and untrue fables, and Timothy is reminded to have nothing to do with godless and silly myths but to train himself in godliness.

Thirdly comes self-training. Paul is here thinking of Christian service as a form of athletic contest, and he often used athletic analogies to drive home the need for spiritual discipline. The minister's own spiritual life does not come automatically: he must train himself in spiritual exercises, since the prize for the good fight is both here and hereafter, for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, holding promise for the present life and also for the life to come.

Fourthly, Timothy is to be an example. There is to be a note of authority in his teaching, and Paul's purpose is to inspire the timid young man to display firmness. Many of the Ephesian Christians, especially the elders, were almost certainly of mature years, and having served under Paul the veteran, some would look with disfavour and contempt on the youthful missionary. As a counter-balance to contempt, Timothy would have to live in an exemplary manner, so that it would become evident that in Christianity authority is contingent upon character and not age.

Fifthly, he was to give himself to his spiritual ministry, attending both to his public ministry and to his private life. The public service is to consist of at least three ministerial essentials: the public reading of Scripture, since it has always been the practice of God's people to read the Word aloud in the congregation; preaching, which is exhortation, including the exposition and application of the passages read and addressed to Christians, preaching to non-Christians being evangelism rather than exhortation; and teaching, which may refer primarily to a more catechetical treatment of the truths of the Christian faith. By faithful adherence to a godly life and to the Word of God, Timothy would save both himself and his hearers from the false teachings.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: Discuss Paul's call to Timothy to faithfulness in 2 Timothy 1:3-18.
theory.idealAnswer:
The remembrance of Timothy inspires the apostle with thanksgiving to God. He is moved by Timothy's love but dwells more on his sincere faith, his salvation and his ministry; and Paul viewed his own faith in Christ not as a break with his Jewish forefathers but in continuity with their faith. As he prayed for Timothy night and day his gratitude kept increasing, for as he sat chained in prison there was little else he could do but pray. He remembers Timothy's tears at their last parting and had longed for the companionship which was such a joy to him; it is interesting to learn that even the great apostle at times became lonely, discouraged and in need of support from fellow Christians.

Convinced that Timothy possessed true faith, Paul urged him to fan into flame his God-given ability for ministry, since God's gift must be used to reach and maintain its full potential. Timothy needed the reminder that God did not give us a spirit of timidity but a spirit of power and love and self-control, because he might have been intimidated by the opposition to Paul and to the gospel, possibly threatened and ashamed at having to defend a prisoner and at the foolishness which they both preached about a despised and crucified Jesus. Such timidity or cowardice has no place in God's service; instead God gives a spirit of power, of love and of self-discipline, and these three virtues supplied by the Holy Spirit should characterise Timothy.

In the call to courage Timothy is told that he should not be ashamed, and would not be if his ministry were marked by those virtues. He would then be able to stand against his opponents and would not be ashamed to testify about the Lord, nor ashamed of Paul His prisoner. Paul exhorted him to join in suffering for the gospel, for it is in such circumstances that the power of God is shown; and he spells out that God saved us and called us to a holy life, a salvation which had nothing to do with a believer's merits but was purely because of God's own purpose and grace.

Timothy was also to guard the truth: to view what he had heard from Paul as the essential outline of sound teaching and to maintain it with faith and love in Christ Jesus. The stewardship of the truth had passed into his hands and he was to pass it on to other faithful Christians, guarding it meanwhile through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. Finally, examples are set side by side. All who were in Asia turned away from Paul, probably fearing for their own safety, forsaking him when he needed them most; over against them stands Onesiphorus, who supported him not only in Ephesus but also in Rome. The negative and positive examples were designed to strengthen Timothy's resolve to stand shoulder to shoulder with Paul.

theory.subject: NT
theory.question: What are the marks of a good workman according to 2 Timothy 2:14-26?
theory.idealAnswer:
The instruction of the previous verses was not for Timothy only: he was to keep reminding others of these things and to charge his people solemnly before the Lord to avoid disputing about words, which does no good but only ruins the hearers.

As for Timothy himself, he was to do his best to be sure he would meet with God's approval, a workman or labourer who does not need to be ashamed. Paul had spoken of shame before men, but shame before God is worse; and Timothy need not fear such shame if he would correctly handle the word of truth. He was also to avoid godless chatter - literally, to shun profane empty utterances - which only advances ungodliness like gangrene, gangrene being the mortification of a part of the body caused when it is cut off from its normal supply of blood and nutrition. Two men are named whose teachings were corrupting the local church, Hymenaeus and Philetus, whom Paul had already delivered over to Satan; these two had wandered away from the truth regarding the crucial doctrine of the resurrection, and according to Paul they destroy the faith of some.

The next mark is that of a clean instrument. Paul uses the metaphor of a household: in a large household are all sorts of containers, some made of gold and silver and others of wood and clay, and more importantly some are for noble purposes and some for ignoble - a reference to the faithful and the unfaithful within the church. The metaphor shows how one can be an instrument for noble purposes by cleansing himself from the ignoble vessels. Timothy was to have nothing to do with the false teachers, and in this way he would be a vessel for noble use, made holy, useful to the master and prepared for any good work. What is clean and set apart for special use can easily get contaminated and rendered unusable through contact with the corrupt, and Paul was concerned that Timothy keep himself in a usable condition for the Lord.

The last mark is faithfulness in conduct. Timothy was to shun youthful passion and aim at righteousness, faith, love and peace. Probably Paul did not have sexual passions primarily in mind: the evil desires of youth would include all the unholy desires that characterise young people, such as self-assertion, love of argument, partiality, intolerance and impatience. The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kindly to everyone, correcting his opponents with gentleness, so that God may perhaps grant that they will repent and come to know the truth. When brethren fall into false teaching they must be treated with gentleness and Christian love in the hope that they will come to their senses and escape from the trap of the devil who has taken them captive; for false teaching is always the handiwork of Satan, but God in His grace often salvages the situation through the Christ-like ministry of His servants.
